l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCSE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson L09: Database data types and validation.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Choose and justify a suitable data type for each field in a table. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

When a database table is designed, every field is given a field name and a data type. The data type decides what kind of data the field can hold and what can be done with it. Short Text is for names, addresses, postcodes and any numbers that are not used in calculations, such as phone numbers. Long Text holds longer descriptions. Number is for numeric values that will be used in calculations, such as the number of people in a group.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Currency is for money and shows two decimal places. Date/Time stores dates and times so that they can be sorted in date order and used to work out ages or due dates. AutoNumber creates a new number automatically for each record and is often used for the key field. Yes/No holds a Boolean value with only two options. Choosing the right data type is the first step in keeping data accurate, because the database will refuse data of the wrong type.
Right. What else do we need to know?

Database packages such as Access offer several more data types. Hyperlink stores a web address or email address that can be clicked. Attachment lets files, such as a photo of a club member, be attached to a record. OLE Object, short for Object Linking and Embedding, stores a file created in another program, such as a spreadsheet or a word-processed document. Calculated holds the result of a calculation that uses other fields in the same record, for example a total cost worked out from the number in the group multiplied by the price per person.
Got it. Keep going.

Lookup Wizard creates a drop-down list of values, so the user picks an answer rather than typing it. In the exam you may need to justify a data type. Give a reason linked to the data. For example, a phone number should be Short Text because it starts with a zero, may contain spaces and is never used in a calculation. Storing it as a Number would drop the leading zero.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

Validation is an automatic check carried out by the computer when data is entered. It makes sure that the data is sensible, reasonable and within acceptable limits. If the data breaks a rule, it is rejected and an error message, called validation text, tells the user what is wrong. Validation matters because a database is only useful if its data is accurate. Wrong or missing data leads to wrong results, for example a letter sent to an incomplete address or a bill calculated from an impossible number of days.
Okay. Keep going.

Validation reduces these input errors. However, validation cannot check that data is correct. It can only check that data is allowed. If a parent's date of birth is typed as 12/05/1984 instead of 21/05/1984, both dates are valid, so the mistake gets through. This is why validation is often combined with verification, such as typing an email address twice, or a visual check against the original document.
Go on.

A presence check makes sure a field is not left blank. It suits fields that every record must have, such as a customer's surname or postcode. A length check makes sure the data has the right number of characters. It can set an exact length, such as a seven-character camper code, or a minimum or maximum, such as a password of at least eight characters.
Right. Keep going.

A type check makes sure the data is of the correct data type, so letters cannot be typed into a Number or Date/Time field. A format check makes sure the data matches a set pattern, such as a Northern Ireland postcode that starts with BT followed by digits, a space, a digit and two letters. A range check makes sure a value lies between a lower limit and an upper limit, for example from 1 to 5 days at a summer camp or a test mark from 0 to 100. When answering, always name the check and then describe it using the field in the question.
Go on.

In Access, most checks are set in the field properties in Design View. For a presence check, set Required to Yes, or enter the validation rule Is Not Null. For a length check, set the Field Size, or write a rule using the Len function, such as Len([Password]) greater than or equal to 8, which counts the characters in the field. A type check happens automatically once the data type is chosen.
Makes sense. Keep going.

For a format check, use an input mask. In a mask, L means a letter must be typed, 0 means a digit must be typed and 9 means a digit is optional, so the mask BT09 0LL fits Northern Ireland postcodes. For a range check, write a rule with comparison operators, such as greater than or equal to 1 And less than or equal to 5, or use Between 1 And 5, which includes both end values. Always add validation text that explains the rule in plain English, so the user knows how to fix the error rather than just seeing that it was rejected.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
Data type?
The kind of data a field can hold, e dot g. Short Text, Number, Currency or Date/Time. It controls what can be entered and what can be done with the data.
Validation?

An automatic check made by the computer as data is input, to make sure the data is sensible, reasonable and inside allowed limits. Data that breaks the rules is rejected; validation cannot confirm the data is correct.
Presence check?
A check that makes sure data has been entered in a required field, so the field cannot be left blank.
Length check?
A check that makes sure the data entered has an exact number of characters, or is no shorter or longer than set limits.
Type check?
A check that makes sure the data entered is of the correct data type, e dot g. numeric, text or date.
Format check?
A check that makes sure the data entered matches a set pattern, e dot g. a postcode or an email address containing @.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Data types and validation have come up often: the 2019 paper, question 3 and the 2024 paper, question 3 asked for data types with a justification, the 2022 paper, question 10 covered field types and validation, the 2021 paper, question 2 asked about presence and range checks, the 2023 paper, question 3 asked for validation rules, and the 2025 paper, question 5 covered data types and validation checks. Most marks come in pairs: one mark for naming the check or data type and one for a reason or description in context. 'Range check' alone will rarely get both marks; 'a range check so that the number of days booked must be from 1 to 5' will. In 2025 many candidates did not realise that validation cannot tell whether data is correct, so learn that point. When writing a rule, check the boundaries carefully: for 5 to 20 people, greater than or equal to 5 And less than or equal to 20 is right, while >5 And <20 wrongly rejects 5 and 20. Do not confuse a length check, which counts characters, with a range check, which compares values.
Let's finish with a question for the listeners. Which data type is best for a monthly club fee of 24.99 pounds? Is it A, Currency; B, Number (integer); C, Short Text; D, Date/Time?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is A: Currency. Currency is for money and stores two decimal places. An integer would lose the pence.
